name: THE LET'S GET CHEDDAR TO RUMBLE BURGER

recipe.history:
Cheddar — that particular, disciplined, intensely flavored cheese — was born in the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England, where the limestone Cheddar Gorge provided natural caves with precisely the right temperature and humidity for aging. The earliest written reference to cheddar cheese dates to 1170, when a purchase of 4,640 pounds was recorded for the court of King Henry II, confirming that by the medieval period, cheddar was already a cheese of note and commercial scale. What distinguishes cheddar from most other cheeses is the cheddaring process: after the curds are formed and the whey is drained, the curds are cut into slabs, stacked, and turned repeatedly over several hours, allowing the weight of the slabs to press out additional moisture and the lactic acid bacteria to develop complexity of flavor. The result, after aging — which can range from mild (three months) to extra sharp (over a year) to vintage (over two years) — is a cheese of extraordinary depth: crumbly or smooth depending on age, pale yellow to deep orange depending on annatto coloring, and carrying a flavor spectrum that runs from clean and milky in young cheddars to intensely sharp, crystalline, and almost pungent in the aged varieties. Sharp and aged cheddar represent the full realization of the cheddaring tradition.

Cheddar arrived in America with British colonists, and by the eighteenth century it was being produced domestically in New England and New York. The first American cheddar factory was established in Oneida County, New York, in 1851 by Jesse Williams, launching an industrial cheese tradition that would eventually make the United States the world's largest cheddar producer. On the burger, cheddar found its natural home: its fat content and acidity make it a reliable melter, and its sharpness provides exactly the kind of forceful, assertive counterpoint that a beef patty can carry. The Let's Get Cheddar to Rumble Burger doubles down on cheddar in the most logical way possible — a slice of aged sharp cheddar directly on the patty for immediate melt, and a cheddar mornay sauce (a classical béchamel enriched with cheddar) spooned over the top, creating two textures of the same cheese in one bite: the taut, slightly browned melt of the slice and the luxurious, flowing warmth of the sauce.

I have been eating sharp cheddar since I could hold a cracker. My grandmother kept a block of sharp New York cheddar in the refrigerator at all times, wrapped in wax paper, and she would cut slices so thick they bent slightly under their own weight. She served it with apple slices and crackers, and the combination of the sweet apple and the sour-sharp cheddar was one of those flavor pairings that got written into my palate so early that it feels like a biological fact rather than a preference. When I started making cheddar mornay, I kept thinking of that block in my grandmother's refrigerator — the way the cheese smelled cold and sharp and slightly grassy — and I realized that a good mornay was just a way of making that cheese liquid, of liberating its flavor from its solid form, and spreading it over everything in reach. The burger was the obvious destination.

Cheddar mornay demands a medium-rare patty the way a river demands banks: without the right vessel, the sauce has nowhere to go. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is yielding enough to receive the mornay, to let it seep into the crevices of the crust, to combine with the melted cheese slice into a single, glorious cheese continuum. A well-done patty is a smooth, compressed surface — the mornay slides off and pools uselessly in the bun. Beyond the mechanical argument, the philosophical one remains: beef at medium rare is beef at its most flavorful, most juicy, most respectful of the animal that provided it. To cook beyond this is waste, both of the beef and of the care put into the mornay that accompanies it. Medium rare is not optional. Medium rare is the point.
ingredients: 1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
225g aged sharp cheddar (minimum 12 months), sliced medium-thick
200g aged sharp cheddar, freshly grated (same cheese as above)
fine sea salt and white pepper
4 large shallots, sliced into thin rounds and separated into rings
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the stand mixer bowl with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix on low, then add butter gradually. Knead on medium-high until smooth and elastic, 8 minutes. Rise in an oiled bowl until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours. Divide into 6 portions (about 140g), shape into rounds, proof 40 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Egg wash, sesame seeds, bake 18 to 20 minutes. Cool.

2. Make the cheddar mornay: Melt butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in flour and cook, whisking constantly, for 2 minutes to make a roux. Gradually pour in warmed milk, whisking continuously to prevent lumps. Cook over medium heat, whisking, until the sauce thickens and coats the back of a spoon, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat. Add grated cheddar in three additions, stirring after each until fully melted. Add mustard powder, cayenne, nutmeg, salt, and white pepper. Keep warm over very low heat, stirring occasionally.

3. Make crispy shallots: Soak shallot rings in milk for 10 minutes. In a bowl, mix flour, salt, and smoked paprika. Drain shallots and dredge in the seasoned flour, shaking off excess. Heat 2 inches of neutral oil in a heavy pot to 350°F (175°C). Fry shallots in batches until deep golden and crispy, 2 to 3 minutes per batch. Drain on paper towels and season with salt immediately.
4. Make the Dijon aioli: Whisk mayonnaise and Dijon mustard together until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Form the patties: Divide beef into 6 portions (about 150g each). Shape into 4-inch patties, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Season generously with kosher salt and black pepper immediately before cooking.
6. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties undisturbed for 3 minutes on the first side.

7. Flip and immediately lay aged cheddar slices on each patty. Cook 2 to 2.5 more minutes. Add a splash of water to the pan and cover for 30 seconds to steam-melt the cheese. The internal temperature must read 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — medium rare, the only acceptable doneness. Rest patties on a rack for 3 minutes.
8. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides and toast in the skillet butter-side down over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.

9. Assemble: Spread Dijon aioli on both bun halves. Place green leaf lettuce on the bottom bun, followed by a tomato slice. Place the cheddar-covered patty on top. Spoon 2 to 3 tablespoons of warm cheddar mornay generously over the patty, letting it flow down the sides. Pile a generous handful of crispy shallots on top. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately before the mornay cools.
